title: Quantum Chebyshev Transform: Mapping, Embedding, Learning and Sampling Distributions
abstract_summary: The authors introduce a framework for building quantum models in an orthonormal Chebyshev polynomial basis, including an x-parameterized embedding (isometry) that prepares states with amplitudes given by Chebyshev polynomials and a quantum Chebyshev transform circuit that maps between computational and Chebyshev bases. The approach supports exponentially large polynomial degrees, enables automatic differentiation of models, and is applied to generative modeling and efficient sampling of distributions relevant to physics and finance (e.g., log-normal asset-price distributions).
methodology_description: The authors develop a theoretical and simulation-based methodology to construct quantum models in a Chebyshev polynomial basis. They define an orthonormal Chebyshev feature map (an x-parameterized isometry) that prepares quantum states whose amplitudes are Chebyshev polynomials, and they design a quantum Chebyshev transform (QChT) circuit that maps between the computational basis and the Chebyshev basis (related to a type-II discrete cosine transform implemented via an extended QFT plus phase/permutation circuitry). For learning experiments they employ the Differentiable Quantum Generative Model (DQGM) framework: variationally trainable circuits V_theta are trained in the Chebyshev (latent) space using a mean-squared-error loss to approximate target probability densities (synthetic distributions), then the trained model is mapped to the computational basis via the QChT and sampled. Derivatives of the Chebyshev embedding are handled either by parameter-shift rules (noting a 4N shift count for the presented encoding) or by representing the derivative as a linear combination of Chebyshev polynomials and implementing the effective non-unitary derivative operator with LCU-type techniques. All presented experiments are simulated using Julia's Yao.jl package; reported examples include fitting a Black–Scholes log-normal distribution (N=5 qubits) and a simple linear density (N=2 qubits), with specified ansatz depths, learning rate, epochs, training grids (Chebyshev nodes and midpoints), and sampling performed after mapping with the QChT.

Train V_theta variationally in latent Chebyshev space using mean-squared-error loss between model outputs and target PDF values evaluated on the Chebyshev training grid.
Training hyperparameters: learning rate 0.005, simulated for 5000 epochs (as reported for the lognormal example).

For derivative evaluation during training or for physics-informed constraints: use parameter-shift rule (4N shifts for the presented encoding) or implement effective derivative operator via LCU using Chebyshev polynomial derivative identities.
After training, map the learned latent model to the computational basis by applying the quantum Chebyshev transform U_QChT (constructed from QFT plus phase/permutation and local rotations).
Sample the mapped state by performing projective measurements in the computational basis to generate histograms of the learned distribution.

key_findings: [supported] The authors introduce an orthonormal Chebyshev feature map (an x-parameterized isometry) that prepares quantum states whose amplitudes are Chebyshev polynomials and which are orthonormal at the Chebyshev nodes.
[supported] An analytic orthogonality relation (Eq. 3 and related expressions) is provided showing the Chebyshev states |τ(xCh_j)⟩ are orthonormal on the Chebyshev grid.

[supported] The paper presents a concrete quantum Chebyshev transform (QChT) circuit (built from an N+1-qubit QFT plus phase-adjustment, permutation, and controlled rotations) that maps computational basis states to Chebyshev-basis states and vice versa.

[supported] The authors show that the Chebyshev embedding produces amplitudes corresponding to Chebyshev polynomials whose degree scales exponentially with system size (providing exponentially large polynomial degree capacity in the prepared states).

[supported] Methods for differentiating Chebyshev models are described: (i) parameter-shift based differentiation (noting 4N shifts for the orthonormal Chebyshev map under the stated decomposition) and (ii) an LCU/effective-operator approach based on relations between Chebyshev polynomials and their derivatives.

[supported] Numerical simulations demonstrate variational training in the Chebyshev latent space: (i) learning a lognormal distribution using N=5 qubits (hardware-efficient ansatz depth 14, trained for 5000 epochs with lr=0.005) and subsequent sampling via QChT, and (ii) learning a linear target distribution with N=2 qubits where the Chebyshev model better matched the target derivative than a Fourier-based model in the reported experiments.

[supported] The authors show sampling from a trained Chebyshev model can be performed on an extended computational register (example: mapping a trained 2-qubit model to 8 qubits via QChT and sampling), and provide plotted histograms from simulations (including a 10^6-shot sampling histogram in one figure).

[speculative] The authors propose several potential applications/extensions (solving differential equations, amplitude-loading for linear-system solvers, PDE/ODE spectral methods, multivariate embeddings via parallel reuploading, and links to quantum-walk/hamiltonian encodings), but these remain conceptual/proposed and are not empirically validated in the paper.

results_summary: This preprint proposes a framework for quantum model building using an orthonormal Chebyshev basis. The authors design an x-parameterized isometry (Chebyshev feature map) that prepares states with Chebyshev-polynomial amplitudes, provide analytic orthogonality at Chebyshev nodes, and give a concrete quantum Chebyshev transform (QChT) circuit to map between computational and Chebyshev bases. They describe differentiation strategies (parameter-shift and LCU-based effective operators) and demonstrate with numerical simulations that variational models trained in the Chebyshev latent space can learn and be sampled as target distributions (examples: a lognormal distribution with N=5 qubits and a linear distribution with N=2, including comparisons showing better derivative fidelity versus a Fourier embedding). The paper discusses possible applications such as generative modeling, spectral PDE/ODE solvers, amplitude encoding, and multivariate embeddings, but these are presented as proposals rather than experimentally validated advantages.
